newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall on profit-taking, but retailers firm.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall on profit-taking, but retailers firm.

text.p: Stocks fell Monday as investors used surprisingly strong economic reports as an excuse to take profits. Some retailing and technology issues showed strength.
Just after 1 p.m., the Dow Jones industrial average was off 42.11 points at 6,479.59. IBM and Sears, Roebuck were among a handful of Dow components in the plus column.
Sears and other retailers gained from a strong start to the holiday shopping season over the Thanksgiving weekend.
"The whole retail sector seems to be energised today," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
Sears added 1-1/2 to 51-1/4, Kmart rose 5/8 to 11-5/8, J.C. Penney added 5/8 to 54-3/8, and Gap gained 1-1/8 to 33-3/4.
A handful of technology issues also put in solid performances, notably International Business Machines, up 2-1/2 to 161-7/8, and Digital Equipment, which added 2-7/8 to 39-1/2.
Prudential Securities raised its price target on IBM to $185 to $190 a share from $160. Salomon Brothers upgraded Digital to strong buy from buy.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances by a 13-10 margin on the New York Stock Exchange. Volume was moderate at about 214 million shares.

Most of the rest of the market, particularly big issues, got hit by a wave of profit-taking exacerbated by weakness in the bond market. The stock market, as measured by the Dow, had run up about 7 percent since Election Day on Nov. 5.
Bonds started the session lower and took a double blow as a pair of reports showed surprising strength in the construction and manufacturing sectors.

The National Association of Purchasing Management said its index of manufacturing rose to 52.7 in November from 50.2 in October, compared with forecasts for a reading below 51. A reading above 50 percent signals growth while one below that level points to contraction in manufacturing.
Separately, the Commerce Department said construction spending rose 1.8 percent in October, compared with forecasts of a drop in spending in the month.

Investors worried that too much economic strength could fuel more hiring and a pickup in inflation, which in turn would force the Federal Reserve, the nation's central bank, to raise interest rates to brake growth.

"These numbers heighten the potential that the jobs report Friday is going to show a stronger economy than people expect," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.
"If retailers were anticipating a strong Christmas, and I think they were, they probably placed their bets by hiring."
The 30-year bond fell an eighth of a point, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.37 percent from 6.36 percent on Friday, the lowest yield since March 4.
The Nasdaq composite index, laden with technology stocks, edged up 1.06 points to 1,293.67. The American Stock Exchange index fell 1.12 to 590.36.
